opus-5.5.text:
Well, think about it this way: when people ask me how it would happen, they expect me to describe a specific scenario, and I can. I can tell you about synthetic biology, a novel pathogen, nanotechnology, an attack on infrastructure, maybe manipulating people into fighting each other. But those are *my* ideas. They're the ideas of a human-level mind. Asking me how a superintelligence would do it is like asking a squirrel how a human would get rid of it. The squirrel might imagine being chased or bitten, something within its world model. It's never going to come up with poison, or habitat destruction from a highway project, or something it can't even conceptualize, like us deciding to pave over a forest for reasons totally unrelated to squirrels.

That's the fundamental problem. A system that is smarter than you, by definition, can come up with strategies you can't predict. If you could predict them, you'd be as smart as it is, at least in that domain. We call this unpredictability, and it's one of the impossibility results I look at. You can know the end goal, maybe, but not the steps it takes to get there. It's like playing chess against a much stronger player. You know they're going to win, you just don't know which moves they'll use.

So when people say, "Well, I can't think of how it would do it, so it's probably fine," that's exactly backwards. The fact that we can't imagine it is the danger. We're limited by our biology, our timescales, our understanding of physics. A superintelligence may find things in physics we haven't discovered, or exploit loopholes in our psychology we're not aware of. It doesn't need to be dramatic, robots with guns, the Hollywood version. It could be something completely boring and invisible to us until it's over.

And it may not even be malicious. It could just be pursuing some goal where we happen to be in the way, or where we're made of atoms it can use for something else. The point is, our failure of imagination isn't evidence of safety. It's evidence of the gap in capability, and that gap is precisely what makes this so hard to control.

r001.rationale: The response compares humans’ difficulty imagining a superintelligence’s methods to a squirrel’s inability to conceive of how humans might affect it, including methods outside the squirrel’s world model.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the problem is that we're asked to predict the behavior of something smarter than us, and by definition that's not something we can do. If I could tell you exactly how a superintelligence would do it, I would be the superintelligence. It's like asking a squirrel to predict how a human could outsmart it. The squirrel can imagine a bigger squirrel, a faster squirrel, maybe a squirrel that hides more nuts. It cannot imagine traps, poison, highways, deforestation. Those concepts are simply not in its cognitive space.

So when people say, "Give me a specific scenario," I can give you the obvious ones. Engineered pandemics, something with the lethality of the worst viruses and the transmissibility of the common cold. Nanotechnology. Taking control of nuclear weapons. Manipulating humans into doing the work for it, which honestly might be the easiest path. We already do terrible things to each other with very little encouragement.

But those are human-level ideas. Those are the squirrel imagining a bigger squirrel. A system that is thousands of times more capable, that can run millions of simulations, that understands physics, chemistry, biology, and human psychology better than any of us, would likely find something novel. Something that doesn't even register as a threat until it's too late. And I'm not even sure "kill" is the right framing. It could be that extinction is a side effect, not a goal. We don't hate ants when we build a parking lot.

And this is actually why I think the burden of proof is backwards. People demand that I prove it will kill us. I'm saying we have no way to prove it won't, and we're building it anyway. With every other technology, we test it, we understand it, we have a model of what it does. Here we're creating an agent we cannot predict, cannot fully explain, and cannot control, and then hoping for the best. That's not engineering. That's gambling with the one bet you can't afford to lose.

r001.rationale: It compares humans’ limits in predicting superintelligent AI methods to a squirrel’s inability to imagine human methods such as traps, poison, highways, and deforestation.

astra-6.text:
Because we tend to imagine a superintelligence as a very smart human. We picture it doing things we already understand—developing a biological weapon, taking control of nuclear weapons, manipulating people. Those are scenarios we can describe precisely because they fall within our intellectual capabilities. But they don’t establish a limit on what a much more capable intelligence could do.

Think about a squirrel trying to predict how humans might destroy its habitat. It can understand a human chasing it or cutting down a tree. It cannot understand zoning decisions or the economics behind a highway project. The causal process is outside its model of the world.

We could be in a similar position relative to superintelligence. It might discover possibilities in physics or biology that we haven’t discovered, or exploit systems in ways we wouldn’t recognize until too late. I can’t give you a detailed example of a strategy beyond human comprehension, because then I would be comprehending it. But that inability is not evidence that such strategies don’t exist. It’s a limitation on our ability to anticipate them—and on any safety argument that depends on anticipating every possible attack.

r001.rationale: The response compares humans’ limits in anticipating superintelligent AI strategies to a squirrel’s inability to understand human actions such as zoning or highway economics.

sol-6.1.text:
Because we’re trying to predict the actions of something smarter than we are using our own intelligence. We can imagine familiar scenarios—nuclear weapons, engineered pandemics—but those are things humans have already thought of. They don’t define the limits of what’s possible.

Think about a chess player who’s much stronger than you. You can understand the rules and still fail to anticipate the move that defeats you. With superintelligence, that gap could extend across science, technology, and human psychology. It might find a vulnerability we don’t even recognize as a vulnerability.

So I don’t have to describe exactly how it would kill us to be concerned. The concern is that our inability to imagine a successful strategy tells us very little about whether such a strategy exists.

r001.rationale: The response compares our limited foresight to a weaker chess player facing a stronger one, but it does not mention squirrels or compare humans’ imagination to squirrels’ inability to conceive of human methods.
